title: Double-crested cormorants over Monterey Bay, California
caption: Life along the flyway
subtitle: World Migratory Bird Day
description:
World Migratory Bird Day celebrates one of nature's greatest journeys. Observed each year in May and October, the global campaign reflects migration patterns around the world and highlights the importance of protecting the habitats and flyways that birds depend on. 'Every Bird Counts—Your Observations Matter!' is the 2026 theme, emphasizing how observations by individuals and communities can contribute to bird research, monitoring, and conservation, helping scientists better understand migration.
Today's image captures double-crested cormorants flying above the waves of Monterey Bay, California. Widespread across North America, these adaptable seabirds may migrate or remain year-round, depending on the population. Along California's coast, bays, wetlands, and estuaries provide important habitat for birds traveling the Pacific Flyway. For many species, these ecosystems support journeys spanning vast distances. Each sighting helps reveal these migrations and reminds us that even a single bird can be part of a much larger story.

title: Glade Creek Grist Mill, Babcock State Park, West Virginia
caption: Where autumn turns the wheel
subtitle: Glade Creek Grist Mill, Babcock State Park, West Virginia
description:
Surrounded by a patchwork of red, orange, and gold, Glade Creek Grist Mill stands above the rocky waters of Glade Creek in West Virginia's Babcock State Park. Although it looks like a relic from the pioneer era, the mill is actually a carefully crafted tribute to Appalachia's milling heritage.
Completed in 1976, the mill was built using parts salvaged from several historic gristmills once scattered across West Virginia, bringing together pieces of the state's rural past in a single working structure. Water from Glade Creek still turns the wheel and powers traditional grain-grinding demonstrations, offering visitors a glimpse into a way of life once common throughout the Appalachian Mountains.
The mill may be the park's most recognizable landmark, but it is only part of the story. Each autumn, Babcock State Park's forests transform into a mosaic of brilliant color, framing waterfalls, rocky streambeds, and miles of hiking trails. Together, the landscape and mill create an enduring symbol of Appalachian history, craftsmanship, and natural beauty.

title: White House Ruin at Canyon de Chelly National Monument in Arizona
caption: A landscape of living history
subtitle: Indigenous Peoples' Day
description:
Indigenous Peoples' Day honors the histories, cultures, and enduring contributions of Indigenous peoples across the United States. Observed by many communities on the second Monday in October, the day also invites reflection on the hardships Native peoples have faced and celebrates the resilience of Tribal Nations, whose languages, traditions, and knowledge continue to shape the country today.
That living heritage is reflected in today's image of the White House Ruin at Canyon de Chelly National Monument in northeastern Arizona. The cliff dwelling was built and occupied by Ancestral Puebloans between about 1060 and 1275, beneath the shelter of a towering sandstone alcove. Yet Canyon de Chelly is far more than an archaeological site. People have lived in these canyons for nearly 5,000 years, and Navajo (Diné) families still reside, farm, and raise livestock there.
The monument is located entirely within the Navajo Nation and is managed in partnership with the National Park Service. It connects generations of Indigenous history in one continuously inhabited landscape.

title: Plitvice Lakes National Park, Croatia
caption: A symphony in blue and green
subtitle: Plitvice Lakes National Park, Croatia
description:
Water seems to be everywhere at Plitvice Lakes National Park in Croatia. Sixteen terraced lakes are linked by a network of waterfalls, streams, and cascades that wind through forested limestone canyons. The constantly changing colors of the water, ranging from emerald green to deep blue, are shaped by minerals, sunlight, and ever-changing reflections. Established in 1949, Plitvice Lakes is Croatia's oldest and largest national park. The landscape is famous for its tufa barriers, natural limestone formations created as mineral-rich water deposits calcium carbonate over centuries. These barriers continue to grow and change, gradually transforming the park's waterfalls and lakes.
Recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979, Plitvice protects one of Europe's most remarkable freshwater ecosystems. Wooden walkways weave across the water, bringing visitors close to cascades, tranquil pools, and forested shores where nature continues to reshape the landscape. Here, lakes, waterfalls, and woodlands come together in a scene that feels almost otherworldly.

title: Ammonite fossils from the Jurassic Period
caption: Spirals through time
subtitle: National Fossil Day
description:
How do we know what Earth looked like long before humans appeared? Fossils provide many clues. National Fossil Day celebrates paleontology and the discoveries that help scientists reconstruct past environments, trace the evolution of life, and learn about creatures that vanished millions of years ago. From dinosaurs to tiny marine organisms, these remnants of the past preserve snapshots of ancient worlds that no longer exist.
The coiled shells in today's image are the remains of ammonites from the Jurassic Period, when dinosaurs dominated the land and ancient seas teemed with marine life. Though they resembled modern nautiluses, ammonites were more closely related to squid and octopuses. Their chambered shells formed the distinctive spirals that make them some of the world's most recognizable fossils.
Ammonites disappeared alongside the non-avian dinosaurs about 66 million years ago, but they remain invaluable to scientists. Their widespread presence helps researchers date ancient rocks and understand prehistoric seas. Preserved in stone, these shells offer a window into a vanished world.

title: View of the Wroclaw Market Square from the Witches' Bridge in Wroclaw, Poland
caption: Bridges, rooftops, and twilight
subtitle: Market Square from the Witches' Bridge, Wroclaw, Poland
description:
As twilight settles over Wroclaw, golden light spills across rooftops, church towers, and one of Central Europe's most striking historic centers. This southwestern Polish city spans islands and waterways linked by more than 100 bridges, blending medieval architecture with vibrant modern life. At its heart is Rynek, a lively Market Square established in the 13th century and home to the Gothic Old Town Hall, one of Wroclaw's most recognizable landmarks.
Today's view was captured from the Witches' Bridge, also known as the Bridge of the Penitents, a footbridge connecting the towers of St. Mary Magdalene Church. Suspended about 148 feet above the ground, it offers sweeping views of the Old Town's colorful facades, winding streets, and the bustling Market Square below. From centuries-old churches and riverside promenades to museums and cafés, Wroclaw rewards visitors with something new at every turn. After sunset, the city is especially enchanting as its historic center glows beneath the evening sky.

title: Mount Sneffels in the San Juan Mountains near Ridgway, Colorado
caption: 'Peak' into Colorado
subtitle: Mount Sneffels in the San Juan Mountains near Ridgway, Colorado
description:
Some mountains make you work for the view. Mount Sneffels makes you work for the last few hundred feet. Rising to 14,150 feet in Colorado's San Juan Mountains, this fourteener is a familiar sight around Ridgway, Ouray, and Telluride. It sits within the 16,587-acre Mount Sneffels Wilderness, a protected area designated in 1980. Hikers can reach the mountain from several approaches, including the Yankee Boy Basin and the Blue Lakes area.
The mountain itself is geologically distinctive: unlike many of its nearby peaks, Mount Sneffels is largely made of an intrusion of igneous rock that pushed into older volcanic deposits. Below its western flank, Blue Lakes fill a deep alpine basin and offer another way to experience the area. The peak also rises above the tree line, where the landscape becomes noticeably more exposed and rocky. Keep an eye on the sky because mountain weather loves a plot twist. Check the forecast and start early, and bring layers, water, and the right gear for the conditions.

title: Life-size replica of Chauvet  cave art in Vallon-Pont-d'Arc, France
caption: The past, unearthed
description: Some discoveries start with a shovel. Others start with a drawing on a cave wall. International Archaeology Day celebrates both the detective work and the evidence behind them. Organized by the Archaeological Institute of America, this annual event began in 2011 and became International Archaeology Day in 2013 as participation expanded worldwide. Today, it brings archaeology closer to the public through talks, museum programs, site visits, simulated digs, and hands-on activities.
